                    ### Question
                    A 22-year-old woman presents to her physician with an increased vaginal discharge. She has no other complaints. She has recently changed her sexual partner, who claims to have no genitourinary symptoms. They do not use condoms. Her vital signs are as follows: blood pressure, 110/80 mm Hg; heart rate, 65/min; respiratory rate, 11/min; and temperature, 36.6℃ (97.9℉). Her physical examination is unremarkable. The gynecologic examination shows increased production of a white-yellow vaginal discharge. Wet mount microscopy shows the below picture. Which of the following treatments is indicated in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Peroral metronidazole
opb. Vaginal clindamycin gel
opc. Peroral cephalexin
opd. No treatment required in the patient with minor symptoms
ope. Vaginal probiotics

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with increased vaginal discharge, which could indicate bacterial vaginosis (BV) or vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC). The wet mount microscopy findings are crucial for diagnosis. If clue cells are present, this suggests BV, for which peroral metronidazole is the first-line treatment. If yeast forms are observed, it indicates VVC, which would require treatment with vaginal clindamycin gel or antifungal agents, but not metronidazole. Given the context of a recent sexual partner change and the absence of other symptoms, the most likely diagnosis is BV, leading to the conclusion that peroral metronidazole is indicated. The option of no treatment may apply if the discharge is physiological, but the presence of increased discharge and the recent sexual history necessitate treatment. Therefore, the best-supported treatment option is peroral metronidazole.
